What Shapes a Kitchen Remodel?
A kitchen can range from a cosmetic refresh to a full gut. Five factors change the scope the most:

items: Cabinets: stock, semi-custom and custom cabinets differ in sizes, finishes and lead times. Choose cabinets and layout first, then design the rest around them.
Countertops: laminate, quartz, granite, quartzite and marble all look and wear differently. Seeing samples in your own light helps more than any chart.
Appliances: their sizes, ventilation and power or gas needs affect the layout, so confirm the models early.
Electrical and plumbing: new lighting, outlets, a relocated sink or a new range location all add work behind the walls.
Structural changes: moving walls or expanding the kitchen footprint is a bigger project than updating what is already there.

Richmond-Specific Factors

Older homes in neighborhoods like Forest Hill, Bon Air, and the Westover Hills area often have aging plumbing (cast iron, galvanized) and knob-and-tube or early aluminum wiring that is usually replaced once the walls are opened for new electrical or plumbing work. If your home is older, plan for the possibility of surprises behind the walls; a walkthrough during your [free estimate](/contact) helps us spot likely ones early.

In Chesterfield County, moving, adding, or removing a wall requires a building permit. Replacing cabinets, plumbing fixtures like sinks and faucets, and floor coverings does not require a permit by itself. The county's permit fees are flat fees, not a percentage of what you spend, and the county publishes its fee schedule. We handle the entire permit process, so you don't have to deal with any of it.

Common Planning Mistakes to Avoid

items: Not leaving room in the plan for surprises such as water damage, code corrections or material changes
Buying appliances first and designing around them; choose cabinets and layout first
Skipping a required permit: Chesterfield charges an extra code investigation fee when work starts without a required permit, and unpermitted work can complicate resale and insurance claims
Choosing a bid only because it is the lowest; compare what each written quote actually includes

content.text: Is a Kitchen Remodel Worth It?

Resale value is only part of the picture. The real return is a kitchen you use every day. A well-planned layout, good lighting and durable materials make daily life easier, and a clear written scope keeps the project on track. title: Do I Need a Permit to Build a Deck in Chesterfield County, VA?
metaTitle: Deck Permit Chesterfield County VA: What to Know | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: Find out when a deck permit is required in Chesterfield County, VA, how the process works, and what happens if you skip it. Licensed contractor explains everything.
imgAlt: Custom deck built by MAS Contractors in Chesterfield County Virginia
excerpt: Building a deck in Chesterfield County? Here's exactly when you need a permit, what the process looks like, and the real risks of skipping it — from a licensed Virginia contractor who pulls permits every week.

content.text: Short answer: Yes. Chesterfield County requires a building permit to build, replace, add to, or structurally repair a deck, whether or not it is attached to the house. Only simple like-for-like work, such as replacing deck boards or handrails, is exempt. Here's what the county says, what the process looks like, and what skipping the permit can cost you.
Need help with this project? See our [Deck & Porch Construction in Richmond, VA](/services/decks-porches).
When Is a Deck Permit Required in Chesterfield County?
Chesterfield's Building Inspection Department enforces the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (USBC) and lists these deck-related projects as requiring a building permit:

items: Building a new deck or porch, including its steps or ramp, whether or not it is attached to the main structure
Replacing a deck or adding to an existing one
Making structural repairs to a deck, such as posts, beams, joists, and footings
Converting an existing deck or porch to a Florida room (sunroom)
Any deck that will carry a hot tub or spa: the county requires a design sealed by a registered design professional showing the deck can support the loads

content.text: What doesn't need a permit: the county's no-permit list includes repairing or replacing deck flooring and repairing or replacing handrails, but a permit is required to repair or replace structural elements or to include posts and guard systems. A separate electrical permit may also be required depending on the scope of work, for example for outlets or lighting. Setbacks from your property lines still apply, so the county asks for a plot plan with every deck application. When in doubt, call Chesterfield County Building Inspection at 804-751-4990, or let us handle it.
What Does the Deck Permit Process Look Like in Chesterfield?

items: Prepare a plot plan showing the deck's location, its dimensions, and its distance from every property line
Prepare two or more copies of construction plans: how the deck attaches to the house, floor framing, footing details, guardrail and picket framing, and post locations and sizes
Submit the Residential Building Permit Application with the plans, and pay the fee at application (currently $114 for a deck, plus a 2% state levy)
Chesterfield Building Inspection reviews the application
Footing inspection: the inspector checks the footings before concrete is placed (it can be combined with the final inspection if you use solid concrete block footings and leave them exposed)
Final inspection: after the deck is complete, the inspector signs off and closes the permit

content.text: MAS Contractors manages every step of this process. We prepare the drawings, submit the application, and schedule the inspections.
How Long Does Chesterfield Permit Approval Take?

Chesterfield County's published goal is to review residential plans within 10 working days, according to its residential requirements pamphlet. Actual timing depends on how complete your plans are and on the project, so we submit full drawings and build review time into every schedule. A deck that needs a sealed design, such as one carrying a hot tub, can take longer. Confirm current timing with Building Inspection.

Planning more than one project? Our guides on [deck planning guide](/blog/deck-cost-richmond-va-2026) and [permit rules for roof replacement and siding](/blog/roof-replacement-siding-permit-chesterfield-county-virginia) are a good next read.

content.title: Get a Free Deck Estimate

What Happens If You Skip the Permit?
This is the part contractors don't always tell you, but we will:

items: Code investigation fee: when work starts without a required permit, Chesterfield charges a fee of the greater of 25% of the permit fee or $57, on top of the normal permit fees.
Criminal penalty: under Virginia Code § 36-106, violating the building code is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $2,500, and a court can order the violation corrected.
Insurance issues: if someone is injured on an unpermitted deck, your insurer may dispute the claim. Check your policy.
Resale problems: real estate agents and home inspectors often flag unpermitted structures, and buyers can ask for a retroactive permit or a price reduction.
Safety risk: permit inspections exist to catch problems with footings and ledger connections before they are covered up. A deck failure injures people.

content.text: Pro tip: Permits protect you, not just the county. A properly permitted and inspected deck gives you legal documentation that it was built to code — which is worth real money at resale.
Who Is Responsible for Pulling the Permit?

Chesterfield allows the property owner, a licensed contractor, or the owner's agent (with the owner's written permission) to apply for a residential permit. Virginia law lets homeowners do work on their own primary residence themselves, but we recommend a licensed contractor for a structure that people will stand on. If a contractor tells you not to worry about the permit, walk away: Virginia requires every residential contract to include the contractor's assurance that they will comply with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements. We pull every permit ourselves and stand behind the work through every inspection.

title: Hardie Board vs. Vinyl Siding: Which Is Better for Virginia's Climate?

content.text: Both Hardie board (fiber cement) and vinyl siding are popular choices in the Richmond area — and both can look great. But Virginia's climate creates specific pressures on siding that make the choice more consequential than in drier parts of the country. Here's what you need to know.
Need help with this project? See our [Siding Installation & Replacement in Chesterfield & Richmond, VA](/services/siding).
What Is Hardie Board (Fiber Cement) Siding?

James Hardie fiber cement siding is made from a blend of cement, sand, and cellulose fibers. It's formed into planks, panels, or shingles that mimic the look of wood with dramatically better durability. MAS Contractors is a certified James Hardie installer — meaning our crews are trained and tested specifically on Hardie products and installation standards.
What Is Vinyl Siding?

Vinyl siding is extruded PVC plastic formed into horizontal or vertical planks. It is one of the most widely installed siding materials in the US, primarily because of its low upfront cost. Modern vinyl has improved significantly from earlier generations, with better UV stabilizers and thicker profiles available at premium price points.

content.text: Why Hardie Board Wins in Virginia's Climate
Virginia's mix of hot, humid summers, freeze-thaw cycles in winter, and active termite populations is hard on siding. Fiber cement handles all three better than vinyl:

items: Humidity: Vinyl can warp when temperatures swing between 95°F summer days and 20°F winter nights. Fiber cement has a much lower expansion coefficient.
Freeze-thaw: Vinyl becomes brittle in sub-freezing temperatures and can crack on impact. Fiber cement remains stable.

Termites: While vinyl isn't food for termites, it's sometimes installed over OSB or wood furring that is. Hardie installed over non-organic materials eliminates termite entry points at the siding level.
Wind and hail: Richmond and Chesterfield see significant storm activity. Fiber cement holds up to hail and wind-driven debris that would dent or crack vinyl.

title: How to Choose a General Contractor in Richmond, VA: 7 Questions to Ask
metaTitle: How to Choose a Contractor in Richmond VA | MAS Contractors Guide
metaDescription: Hiring a general contractor in Richmond VA? Ask these 7 questions before signing anything. A licensed Class A contractor explains what separates great contractors from risky ones.
imgAlt: MAS Contractors team on a residential remodeling project in Richmond Virginia
excerpt: The wrong contractor can turn your dream remodel into a nightmare. Before you sign anything or hand over a deposit, ask every Richmond contractor these 7 questions — and know what the right answers look like.

content.text: Virginia has thousands of licensed contractors and an unknown number of unlicensed ones. The difference between a great experience and a horror story almost always comes down to who you hired and what you didn't ask before signing. Here's the framework we'd want our own family members to use.
1. Are You Licensed in Virginia — and at What Class?

Virginia requires contractors to hold a license from the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation (DPOR) for work over $1,000. The class depends on the value of the contract: Class C for a single contract over $1,000 and under $30,000, Class B from $30,000 up to $150,000, and Class A for $150,000 or more (or $1 million or more of work in a 12-month period). Make sure the contractor's class covers your job: contracting without the proper class for the value of the work is a Class 1 misdemeanor under Virginia law. You can verify any contractor's license on the DPOR website in a couple of minutes. MAS Contractors holds a Class A General Contractor License.
2. Do You Carry General Liability and Workers' Compensation Insurance?

Ask for a Certificate of Insurance — a legitimate contractor will send it without hesitation. General liability protects your property if something is damaged. Workers' compensation protects you if a worker is injured on your property (without it, you could be liable). Both are non-negotiable.
3. Do You Pull the Permits, or Do You Ask Me To?

Red flag: any contractor who asks you to pull the permit yourself as a homeowner, or suggests you skip it entirely. Virginia lets owners do work on their own primary residence, so a homeowner can apply for a permit, but then you, not a licensed contractor, answer for the work. When a licensed contractor pulls the permit, they furnish proof of their license to the building department, and Virginia requires every residential contract to include the contractor's assurance that they will comply with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements.
4. Can You Provide References from Jobs in the Richmond Area?

Ask for 3 references from projects completed in the last 12 months, in the same neighborhood or city if possible. Call them. Ask: Did they finish on time? Were there surprises in the final bill? Would you hire them again? A great contractor will give you references enthusiastically.
5. What Does Your Payment Schedule Look Like?

Virginia requires the written contract to include the progress-payment schedule and a specific statement of the down payment amount. In our experience, legitimate contractors ask for a deposit (typically 10–33% depending on project size) with progress payments tied to completion milestones, and a final payment only after the work is done and you're satisfied. A request for more than half up front is a warning sign. Full payment before the job starts is how scams begin.
6. Will You Use Subcontractors, and Are They Licensed?

Most general contractors use subcontractors for specialized trades (HVAC, electrical, plumbing). That's normal. What you need to know is whether the subs are licensed for their trade in Virginia and covered under the GC's insurance. Ask for confirmation in writing.
7. Will I Receive a Written Contract?

Never hire a contractor based on a verbal agreement or a one-page proposal. Virginia requires residential contractors to use a legible written contract, signed by both parties before work starts or payments are accepted, and to give you a fully executed copy before work begins. At minimum it must state: when work begins and the estimated completion date; the total cost; the progress-payment schedule and the down payment; the materials and work specified; the cancellation rights of both parties; the contractor's name, address, license number, class, and specialties; that any change to cost, materials, work, or completion date must be in writing and signed by all parties; the contractor's assurance of compliance with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements; and a notice about the Virginia Contractor Transaction Recovery Fund. If a contractor resists putting things in writing, walk away.

content.text: What Shortens Roof Life in Virginia's Climate?

items: High humidity: Richmond's humid climate promotes algae, moss, and lichen growth — particularly on north-facing slopes. These organisms don't just stain; the root systems break down shingle granules over time.
Heat cycling: Summer attic temperatures run far above the outdoor temperature. This causes asphalt shingles to expand, contract, and age faster — especially if attic ventilation is inadequate.
Ice dams: While Richmond winters are milder than further north, ice dams can still form during cold snaps. Poor attic insulation and ventilation are the root causes.
Storm damage: Richmond-area summers bring frequent thunderstorms, and the wind and occasional hail they carry wear on shingles over time.
Poor installation: Improperly driven nails, inadequate underlayment, and missing drip edge are common in budget work and can void manufacturer warranties.

content.text: 8 Warning Signs Your Roof Needs Replacing

items: Your roof is 20+ years old and was installed with 3-tab shingles
Shingles are curling at the edges (cupping) or buckling in the middle
Significant granule loss — check your gutters after rain for sand-like debris
Dark stains or streaks (algae) covering large sections of the roof
Daylight visible in the attic — any light means air and water can follow
Sagging or soft spots on the roof deck, visible from the attic or exterior
Multiple areas requiring repairs in the past 2–3 years — patchwork becomes more expensive than replacement
Interior water stains on ceilings, especially after the first freeze-thaw cycle of winter

content.text: Does a roof replacement need a permit? In Chesterfield County, re-roofing and shingle replacement are on the county's list of work that does not require a permit, but structural repairs, such as damaged rafters, do. Virginia's building code also exempts replacing an unlimited amount of roof covering on houses, with a wind-speed condition, and replacing up to 256 square feet of roof decking. Best Time of Year to Replace a Roof in Richmond

Late summer and fall (August–November) are the sweet spot for roof replacements in the Richmond area. Shingle sealant strips are heat-activated, and manufacturers such as Owens Corning publish special procedures for installing shingles at or below 40°F because they may not seal right away. Dry fall weather also reduces the risk of rain delays, and shingles installed in fall have the full winter to seal before the next storm season.

Spring (March–May) is also excellent. Avoid mid-summer installations if possible — 95°F+ temperatures are hard on roofing crews and can cause asphalt shingles to distort during installation if handled improperly.

Pro tip: If you have architectural shingles with an algae-resistance rating, look for the 'AR' designation. Check the manufacturer's warranty terms for the AR rating on the product you choose — it can be worth the small premium for north-facing or heavily shaded roofs in the Richmond area.

title: Planning a Bathroom for How You Live: Layout, Accessibility, Moisture and Durable Finishes
metaTitle: Plan a Bathroom for How You Live: Richmond VA | MAS
metaDescription: Plan a Richmond VA bathroom that works for your daily routine and lasts: layout, accessibility, moisture control, ventilation and durable finishes.
imgAlt: Bathroom remodel completed by MAS Contractors in Richmond VA showing modern tile and fixtures
excerpt: A bathroom planned around your daily routine, and built to handle moisture, will serve you for years. Here is how to think through layout, accessibility, ventilation and finishes.

content.text: The best bathrooms are not the ones with the fanciest finishes. They are the ones planned around how the people in the house actually live, and built to handle water for the long haul. Here is how we think it through with homeowners in Richmond, North Chesterfield, and Henrico. Every job is different and brings its own challenges, so we offer free estimates to see your bathroom first.
Need help with this project? See our [Bathroom Remodeling in Chesterfield & Richmond, VA](/services/bathroom-remodeling).
Start With Your Daily Routine

Before you look at tile, ask who uses this bathroom and when. Two people getting ready at the same time? Children who need a tub? A guest bathroom used once a month? The answers decide whether you want a double vanity, a tub or a walk-in shower, and how much storage matters. Write the answers down and bring them to your [free estimate](/contact); they shape the whole plan.
Layout: Keep What Works, Fix What Does Not

items: Doors and clearances: a door that swings into the toilet or the vanity is an everyday annoyance. A pocket door or an outswing door can free up the room.
Lighting: plan light at the mirror and general light overhead, on dimmers, and avoid a single center fixture that casts shadows on your face.
Storage: a medicine cabinet, a built-in niche in the shower wall, and a linen cabinet keep counters clear.
Moving fixtures: keeping the toilet, shower and vanity where they are keeps the job simpler. If the layout truly does not work, we will go over what moving them involves.

content.text: Accessibility and Aging in Place
A bathroom is one of the first rooms where stairs, slippery floors and tight spaces become a problem. You can plan for that now without making the room look clinical.

items: A low-threshold or curbless shower makes entering easy for everyone.
Blocking inside the walls, installed during the remodel, lets you add grab bars later wherever you need them.
Wider doorways and clear floor space help anyone who uses a walker, a wheelchair, or simply carries a laundry basket.
A full bathroom on the main floor is a real convenience for anyone who has trouble with stairs.

content.text: If you are thinking about a bigger change, such as a main-floor suite, ask about [Home Additions in Richmond, VA](/services/home-additions).
Moisture Control: The Part That Decides How Long It Lasts

Almost every bathroom failure traces back to water in the wrong place. Plan for it in layers: a flat, properly prepared substrate; cement backer board with a proper waterproofing membrane behind tile, never greenboard, which is moisture-resistant but not waterproof; correct slope in the shower floor; and careful sealing around fixtures and penetrations. Our [Tile Installation in Richmond, VA](/services/tile-work) crews spend the most time on exactly the parts you will never see once the tile is up.

Ventilation is the other half. The International Residential Code, which the Virginia Residential Code is based on, sets a minimum bathroom exhaust of 50 cfm for a fan run intermittently (20 cfm if run continuously). Many older fans fall short or are poorly ducted, so we often recommend a quiet, ENERGY STAR fan sized to the room and ducted outdoors. An undersized fan is how a brand-new bathroom ends up with peeling paint and mold. excerpt: Planning a room addition in Chesterfield County? Here's exactly when you need a permit, what the county requires (including when an engineer or soil report is needed), how review works, and the real risks of skipping it — from a licensed Virginia contractor who pulls these permits every month.

content.text: Short answer: Yes. Chesterfield County requires a building permit to build an addition onto an existing house or attached garage. It is also a more involved process than a deck permit: more drawings, a soil report in some areas, and more inspections. Here's what the county requires, what it costs, and why skipping the permit is one of the most expensive mistakes a homeowner can make.
Need help with this project? See our [Home Additions in Richmond, VA](/services/home-additions).
When Is a Permit Required for a Home Addition in Chesterfield County?

Chesterfield's list of projects that require a building permit includes building an addition onto an existing house or attached garage, converting a garage to a habitable space, converting a deck or porch to a Florida room, finishing off an unfinished attic, basement, or room over a garage, and moving, adding, or removing a wall. Under the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (USBC), that covers projects like:

items: Room additions (bedrooms, family rooms, expanded kitchens) on an existing house or attached garage
Second-story additions
In-law suites built as part of the house
Sunrooms and Florida rooms, including converting an existing deck or porch into one
Garage conversions to living space, and finishing an attic, basement, or room over a garage
Any change that moves, adds, or removes a wall, or alters your home's foundation, roofline, or structural framing

content.text: Do You Need an Architect or Engineer for a Home Addition?

Not always. Virginia law does not require an architect or engineer license for the person who prepares plans for single- and two-family homes of up to three stories (Code of Virginia § 54.1-402), and Chesterfield's own guidance says drawings may be prepared by the homeowner or contractor and that a registered architect or engineer is not required for most single-family dwellings. Some items do need an engineer, though. The county requires a sealed soil report showing shrink-swell potential for additions with habitable space in the Triassic basin, and an engineered footing where that potential is moderate or higher. Full-height two-story walls over 12 feet must be engineered by a registered design professional. MAS Contractors coordinates with licensed engineers and soil scientists when your project needs them, so you don't have to source them yourself.

rows: Entire property with property-line dimensions and setbacks from the closest point of the addition
Two or more copies: foundation and footing plan, floor plans, elevations, roof plan, framing, sections, and construction details

content.text: What Does the Home Addition Permit Process Look Like in Chesterfield?

items: Prepare a plot plan showing the proposed addition and its distance from all property lines
Prepare construction drawings (two or more copies): footing and foundation plan, floor plan, elevations, roof plan, framing, and building sections, plus a soil report when required
Submit the application with the plans and pay the permit fees at the time of application
Plan review — the county checks the submission, and other county departments, such as Planning and Environmental Engineering, are part of the approval
Footing inspection — after the trench is dug and reinforcement is installed, before concrete is placed
Foundation inspection — after backfilling the crawl space and before sill plates are placed
Framing inspection — after all structural members are installed and the electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-ins are approved, before anything is concealed
Insulation inspection — after framing is approved and before insulation is covered
Final inspection — after all trade finals are approved, the addition is signed off and the permit closes

content.text: MAS Contractors manages every one of these steps. We submit the application, coordinate the engineer if one is needed, and schedule every inspection — you don't deal with Chesterfield's permit office directly.
How Long Does Chesterfield Permit Review Take for a Home Addition?

Chesterfield County's published goal is to review residential plans within 10 working days, according to its residential requirements pamphlet, but an addition involves more departments and more complex drawings than a deck, and the pamphlet is dated, so confirm current timing with Building Inspection at 804-751-4990. In our experience, plan on several weeks for review and build that time into your schedule. If a soil report is required, order it early, since it has to be submitted with your plans. We submit all documentation in week one of the project so this runs in parallel with material ordering, not on top of it.
How Much Do Home Addition Permits Actually Cost in Chesterfield County?

Unlike your construction budget, permit fees in Chesterfield County are flat fees, not a percentage of what you're spending on the addition itself. Here's the current fee schedule (effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027) for a typical home addition:

Add it up and a typical single-story addition with a new foundation, electrical, and an HVAC extension runs about $1,050–$1,250+ in permit and inspection fees alone — separate from your actual construction cost. A Florida room or attached garage with occupiable space uses a slightly lower base fee ($392 instead of $399); a chimney or porch addition is just $171. These come from the Chesterfield County Department of Building Inspection residential fee schedule for 2026–2027. The county reviews and adjusts them annually, so always confirm the current schedule before finalizing your budget.

Pro tip: permit fees are collected at the time of application, before any work starts — budget for them as a project startup cost, not something you pay at the end. MAS Contractors includes all permit and inspection fees in your written estimate upfront, so there's no separate line item to surprise you mid-project.

What Happens If You Skip the Permit on a Home Addition?
This is where skipping the permit is far riskier on an addition than on a deck — you're not just risking a small structure, you're risking your entire home's legal square footage.

items: Fees and penalties: when work starts without a required permit, Chesterfield charges a code investigation fee (the greater of 25% of the permit fee or $57) on top of the normal fees, and under Virginia Code § 36-106 violating the building code is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $2,500.
Forced corrections: work isn't deemed in compliance until it is inspected and approved (Code of Virginia § 36-105), so unpermitted framing may have to be opened back up for inspection.

Appraisal problems: an addition with no permit history can be flagged by buyers' inspectors and appraisers, and may not be counted the same as permitted finished square footage when you sell or refinance.
Insurance: if a fire, structural failure, or injury happens in an unpermitted addition, your insurer may dispute the claim. Check your policy.
Retroactive permits: many buyers ask for a retroactive permit, which can mean opening finished walls for inspection, at a much higher cost than doing it right the first time.

content.text: Pro tip: the building code requires the permit before the work starts (USBC § 108.1), so a retroactive permit means paying the extra investigation fee and possibly opening finished walls. Doing it right the first time is almost always cheaper.
Who Is Responsible for Pulling the Permit on a Home Addition?

Your general contractor should pull the permit — not you. Any contractor who suggests you pull the permit yourself as a homeowner to save money, or tells you an addition "doesn't really need" a permit, is asking you to take on liability that should be theirs. items: Bathroom shower & floor: Porcelain — tile tested at 0.5% water absorption or less (ASTM C373) can be certified as porcelain, and it generally doesn't need sealing. Check the manufacturer's wear and slip-resistance ratings for wet floors.

Room Addition vs. Home Addition: The Key Difference

A room addition typically means converting or finishing space you already have under roof — a garage conversion, a basement finish, an attic conversion, or a sunroom built onto an existing patio or slab. A home addition means building new square footage from the ground up: a new foundation, new framing, and a new roofline tied into your existing house. Tile is the choice that shapes both the look of the room and the hours of labor in it. Porcelain is the practical default for bathrooms: it needs no sealing and handles humidity well. Natural stone looks beautiful but needs sealing and more upkeep. Large-format tile means fewer grout lines, which helps a small bathroom feel larger and is easier to keep clean. Moisture is what ruins bathrooms, so the exhaust fan deserves as much thought as the tile. excerpt: Most homeowners are surprised to learn that a like-for-like roof or siding replacement usually doesn't need a building permit in Chesterfield County. But "usually" has exceptions. Here's what Virginia's building code and the county actually say, and the cases where a permit is required.

content.text: Short answer: usually no. Under Virginia's building code, replacing your existing roof covering or siding on a house is treated as an ordinary repair, and Chesterfield County lists re-roofing and siding among the work that does not need a permit. But a handful of situations flip that answer to yes: structural repairs, a large amount of roof decking, asbestos-containing materials, and certain historic or flood-zone properties.

Need help with this project? See our [Roofing Services in Chesterfield & Richmond, VA](/services/roofing) and [Siding Installation & Replacement in Chesterfield & Richmond, VA](/services/siding) pages.
What Does Virginia Law Say About Roof and Siding Permits?

Building permits in Virginia come from the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (USBC), which every locality enforces through its own building department (Code of Virginia § 36-105). Section 108.1 of the USBC says a permit is required for the construction or demolition of a building and for alterations involving any structural component, among other things. Section 108.2 then lists work that is exempt, including a category called ordinary repairs.

Two items in that list matter here. First, the code exempts "replacement of an unlimited amount of roof covering or siding" on one- and two-family homes and townhouses, provided the building is not in an area where the nominal design wind speed is greater than 100 mph. Second, it exempts replacing 256 square feet or less of roof decking on those same buildings, unless the decking was originally required to be fire-retardant-treated or otherwise protected as part of a fire-rated assembly.

content.text: What Does Chesterfield County Say?

Chesterfield's Building Inspection Department enforces the USBC and says a building permit is required for most work on your home, "except for some ordinary or minor repairs." Its list of residential work that does not require a permit includes repairing siding, re-roofing and shingles, painting the inside or outside of the house, and installing or replacing gutters and downspouts. Its project requirements page puts installing vinyl siding under cosmetic changes and reroofing under ordinary repairs.
The same pages are just as clear on the other side: any work that is structural in nature requires a permit.

content.text: When Is a Permit Required for a Roof or Siding Job?
In our experience the "yes" answers almost always come from what is found after the old material comes off, not from the plan on paper:

items: Rot in the framing: when old siding or shingles come off and the sheathing is fine, nothing changes. When rafters, trusses, or wall studs have rotted, replacing them is structural work and needs a permit.
More than 256 square feet of decking: a few bad sheets are exempt, but a roof with widespread deck damage can go past the exemption.
Asbestos-containing material: older homes can have cement-board siding or roofing that contains asbestos. Removing or disturbing it requires a permit under the USBC.

Historic districts: the building official may require a permit for replacement siding and roofing inside a locally designated historic district, and the district may have its own material and color rules.
Special flood hazard areas: the building official may require a permit for otherwise-exempt work.

content.caption: Replacing siding like this is treated as an ordinary repair, unless the work uncovers structural damage.

content.text: Pro tip: "no permit" does not mean "no code." The USBC exemptions don't excuse the work from the code's other requirements, so flashing, underlayment, fastening, and ventilation still have to meet it, and a permit-free job also has no county inspection checking them. That is why who does the work matters more when there is no inspector.

There is one more detail worth knowing. When an owner or the owner's agent asks for a permit on exempt work, the code says a permit shall be issued and the related inspections are then required. Some homeowners ask for one on a big job for the paper trail.
How to Confirm Before You Start

items: Check whether your property is in a locally designated historic district or a special flood hazard area. Either can change the answer.
Check your HOA or subdivision covenants. They are separate from the building code and can require approval of roofing and siding materials and colors even when no county permit is needed.
Ask your contractor to inspect the roof deck and framing before quoting a fixed price, because rot and decking damage are what change the permit answer.
If anything is unclear, call Chesterfield County Building Inspection at 804-751-4990 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.) with your address and a short description of the work.

title: Virginia Contractor License: What It Means and How to Verify One
metaTitle: Virginia Contractor License: How to Verify One | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: What a Virginia contractor license means, what a written contract must include and how to check a contractor with DPOR before you hire.
imgAlt: Homeowner checking a contractor license before a remodel in Richmond VA
excerpt: A license is the first thing to check before you hire anyone. Here is what the classes mean, how to look one up on the DPOR site and what a written contract has to include.

content.text: Before you sign anything, check that your contractor is licensed. It takes a few minutes on the DPOR website, and it tells you whether the person you are about to hire is allowed to do the work, which class of license they hold and whether they have a disciplinary record.
What the License Classes Mean

Virginia licenses contractors in three classes, based on the value of a single contract and on the total work a firm takes on in any 12 months. Under § 54.1-1100, Class C covers a single contract over $1,000 but under $30,000. Class B covers $30,000 up to under $150,000. Class A covers $150,000 or more. The law also sets yearly totals for each class, so the contract value is not the only limit.

Electrical, plumbing and HVAC work also requires the right tradesman license. The classes changed in 2025 (Chapter 127 of the 2025 Acts, effective July 1, 2025), so articles written before then may show different amounts.
How to Verify a License on DPOR

items: Open the License Lookup tool on the DPOR website (dpor.virginia.gov/LicenseLookup)
Search by the contractor's name, license number, address or license type. There is also an Advanced License Search
Check that the license is active and that its class fits the size of your project
Use the Disciplinary Action Search tab to see whether the contractor has been disciplined
Ask the contractor for their license number if you do not have it. It must appear in your written contract

content.text: Pro tip: DPOR notes that the data in License Lookup is not the official public record and may not be fully up to date. If something does not match, call the contractor and DPOR before you sign.
What Your Written Contract Must Include

Under the Board for Contractors regulations (18VAC50-22-260), a residential contractor must use a written, legible contract, signed by you and by the contractor before work starts or any payment is accepted. You must receive a signed copy before the work begins. Among other things, it must include:

items: Start and estimated completion dates
The total price and the payment schedule, with a specific statement of the down payment
A list of the work and the materials
A plain-language clause explaining events outside the contractor's control
A statement that the contractor will comply with local permit, inspection and zoning requirements
Your cancellation rights, and the Recovery Fund notice
The contractor's name, address, license number, class of license and specialty
A rule that any change to the price, materials, work or dates must be in writing and signed by everyone

content.text: DPOR's consumer guide also mentions a three-day right to cancel a contract negotiated in your home. It suggests being careful with contractors who ask for full payment up front or who accept only cash or payment apps, and it suggests keeping any initial deposit small.
What Happens If a Contractor Is Not Licensed

Virginia law says no one may do contracting work without a license (§ 54.1-1103). Unlicensed contracting, or contracting without the right class of license, is a Class 1 misdemeanor (§ 54.1-1115), and an unlicensed contractor generally cannot enforce the contract against you, with limited exceptions. The owner exemption in § 54.1-1101 is for owners working on their own property. It does not make it safe to hire someone unlicensed.
The Recovery Fund and How to File a Complaint

The Contractor Transaction Recovery Fund may help eligible consumers who have losses because of improper or dishonest conduct by a licensed residential contractor. It is paid by contractor assessments, not by tax money, and filing a claim does not guarantee payment. You need a court judgment against the licensee, and the contract must be for your Virginia home. State law caps what the Fund pays per claim.

To report a licensee, send DPOR a written report within three years of the violation. Complaints become public once a case is closed. DPOR cannot require a contractor to refund money, so in some cases private legal action is the only way to recover it.
What Is New in 2026

A 2026 law (SB823, approved April 13, 2026) adds required provisions to residential solar contracts. Those rules take effect January 1, 2027 and apply only to solar customers. For other remodeling work, the license classes and contract rules above are the ones that apply.

You are welcome to look up any contractor you are thinking of hiring, including us. For more questions to ask, read [How to Choose a General Contractor in Richmond, VA](/blog/how-to-choose-general-contractor-richmond-va).

metaTitle: Roof Replacement in Richmond VA: What to Know | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: Planning a roof replacement in Richmond VA? Learn about materials, when a permit is needed in Chesterfield and the problems that can come up.
imgAlt: Roof replacement with new shingles on a home in Richmond VA
excerpt: What goes into a roof replacement, when Virginia and Chesterfield County require a permit, and the surprises that can change a roofing job once the old shingles come off.

content.text: A roof replacement looks simple from the street: old shingles off, new shingles on. In practice, every roof is different and brings its own challenges, from the layers underneath to the weather on the day of the job. Here is what goes into one, what the rules say about permits and what can go wrong.
What Goes Into a Roof

Shingles are the part you see, but a roof is a system. A typical replacement includes the roofing material itself, underlayment, waterproofing at the edges and valleys, drip edge, ventilation and flashing around chimneys, vents and walls. Which of these your home needs depends on the roof you have today.

One term worth knowing: roofers measure roofs in squares. Owens Corning's technical page for its Duration shingles lists 3 bundles per square, so a quote that says squares is talking about area, not about the number of bundles on the truck.
Do You Need a Permit?

Under Virginia's statewide building code (13VAC5-63-80, Section 108), replacing any amount of roof covering on a one- or two-family home is exempt from a permit, as long as the home is not in an area where the design wind speed is greater than 100 mph. Replacing 100 square feet or less of roof covering is exempt in all wind zones. The code also lets the local building official require a permit in a locally designated historic district and for exempt work in a special flood hazard area.

Chesterfield County's residential permit page lists re-roofing and shingles among its examples of work that does not require a permit. Henrico and the City of Richmond may handle things differently, so confirm with the local building department before you start.
What Can Go Wrong

items: Surprises under the old shingles: once the roof is open, damaged decking or hidden moisture can appear. Not every problem is visible from the ground or even from the attic.
Color that looks different in person: Owens Corning notes that monitors vary in color and recommends requesting a physical sample. Look at a sample outdoors, next to your siding and trim.
Weather: wet or very windy days stop roofing work, so schedules move. An open roof needs to be protected the same day.
Special locations: historic districts, flood zones and high-wind areas can add requirements, as the code above shows.
Mixing up materials: shingles, underlayment, vents and flashing need to work together. Mixing parts from different systems can cause problems that show up years later.

Roofing materials are sold at home improvement stores and through roofing supply houses. Some suppliers, such as ABC Supply, describe themselves as serving contractors. If you are comparing offers, ask each company which products they plan to use, so you are comparing the same thing.

metaTitle: Siding in Richmond VA: Materials and Pitfalls | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: Fiber cement or vinyl siding in Richmond VA? Learn how each is installed, what can go wrong and when a permit is needed in Chesterfield.
imgAlt: New fiber cement siding installed on a home in Richmond VA
excerpt: Fiber cement and vinyl each have their own rules for cutting, painting and fastening. Here is what manufacturers say to watch for, and what to ask before you choose.

content.text: Siding changes how your home looks and how it handles water, sun and temperature swings. Fiber cement and vinyl are both common in Richmond, and each has its own installation rules. Every house brings its own challenges, so here is what the manufacturers and public sources say to plan for.
For a side-by-side comparison of the two materials, read [Hardie Board vs. Vinyl Siding in Virginia](/blog/hardie-board-vs-vinyl-siding-virginia). This article focuses on what can go wrong.
Do You Need a Permit?

Virginia's statewide building code (13VAC5-63-80, Section 108) exempts replacing any amount of siding on a one- or two-family home from a permit, as long as the home is not in an area where the design wind speed is greater than 100 mph. The local building official may require a permit for replacement siding in a locally designated historic district.

Chesterfield County's pages list repairing siding and installing vinyl siding among the work that does not require a permit. They do not say anything specific about replacing all of a home's siding with another material, so ask the county before you start. Henrico and the City of Richmond may differ.
Fiber Cement (James Hardie): What to Plan For

items: Silica dust: Hardie's installation document says its products contain respirable crystalline silica. It calls for cutting outdoors with good ventilation, using fiber cement shears or a dust-reducing saw connected to a HEPA vacuum, wearing a NIOSH-approved N-95 or better mask and never dry sweeping. It also says never to use a power saw indoors.
Painting window: the same document says products must be painted within 180 days if primed and 90 days if unprimed, with 100% acrylic paint, and that all cut edges must be caulked, painted or primed.
Storage: store the product flat, dry and covered. Installing siding wet may cause shrinkage at butt joints.

Pre-finished color: for ColorPlus products, use only James Hardie touch-up kits. Hardie's warranty excludes third-party paints and defines excess color change by a technical measurement that Hardie decides. If a large area needs touch-up, Hardie says to replace the damaged area with new siding.

Warranty: Hardie's warranty excludes damage from improper storage, handling or installation. Follow the current installation instructions that come with the product. The document we read is dated 2013.

content.text: Vinyl: What to Plan For

items: It moves: the Vinyl Siding Institute manual says vinyl can expand and contract 1/2 inch or more over a 12 ft 6 in length with normal temperature changes.
Fasteners: do not drive the fastener tight against the nail hem. Leave about 1/32 inch of clearance. Do not face-nail or staple through the siding, since it can cause ripples.
Clearance: leave at least 1/4 inch at openings and stops, and 3/8 inch when it is below 40°F.
Water barrier: vinyl is an exterior cladding, not a water-resistive barrier. It must be installed over one.

content.text: Older Homes: Asbestos

The U.S. EPA says asbestos may be found in roofing and siding shingles, and that exposure may occur only when the material is disturbed or damaged. Home repair and remodeling can disturb it. If your home is older and your siding is original, tell your contractor before any cutting or removal begins.
Where to Buy

James Hardie products are sold through dealers and suppliers, and the company has a dealer locator on its Pros Hub page. Vinyl is sold by many suppliers. Prices change often and vary by store, color and profile, so the table below is a snapshot. The best way to compare is to ask each contractor for the brand, product line and trim in writing.
Pro tip: Ask whether the siding will be primed, pre-finished or unpainted, and who is responsible for the paint schedule. Fiber cement has a painting deadline that is easy to miss.
